questions.text: In 'Forgot password', what does 'look up user' do when the email is not in Postgres? Does the flow stop, and does the user see anything different?
questions.about: Forgot password: submit email -> look up user

questions.text: What exactly is rate limited: per email, per IP, or both? Where is the counter stored, and what does the user get back when they hit the limit?
What does 'create token' do step by step? What goes in the reset_tokens row, and what happens to any older unused token for the same user?
What is sent to the Email queue, and does the API respond before or after the email is actually sent? What does the user see if the queue or worker is down?
What does 'the usual retries' mean for the Email worker? How many attempts, what delay, and what happens after the last one fails?
questions.about: The email worker has the usual retries

questions.text: 'Open link' validates the token, then 'Set password' validates it again. Does opening the link use up the token, or only saving the password? What does the user see for an expired or already-used token?
questions.about: Open link: validate token / Set password: validate token

questions.text: How does the server match the token in the link to the stored hash, and how does it know which user the token belongs to?
questions.about: Tokens are random and stored hashed (SHA-256)

questions.text: What does 'revoke sessions' do to the sessions table, and does it include the browser that is doing the reset? Does the user end up logged in or not?
In 'Set password', if the password fails the check (too short or in the breached list), is the token still usable? Where does the breached-list check get its data?

answers.text: The brief says an unknown address gets the same generic message as a real one and nothing is sent. The flow stops after the lookup. The user sees no difference.

The limit is per account, as the brief says. Per-IP limiting is not in the brief and is not added. The counter is not a separate table: it counts reset_tokens rows for the user created in the last hour, including revoked and used rows. A request over the limit creates no row and gets the same generic message.

Step by step: (1) count the user's reset_tokens rows from the last hour; over 3 means stop. (2) Generate 32 random bytes and encode them for the URL. (3) Compute the SHA-256 hash of the raw bytes. (4) In one transaction, set revoked_at on the user's older unused rows and insert the new row with user_id, token_hash, created_at, expires_at = created_at + 30 minutes, and empty used_at and revoked_at. Older rows are kept, not deleted, so the count still works.

The API adds the email job to the queue and then returns the generic message. It does not wait for the mail to be sent. The job carries the address and the link with the raw token. If the queue or worker is down and the enqueue fails, the API still returns the generic message, so the response does not reveal whether the account exists, and it logs the error. The new row is never used and expires after 30 minutes. The user must ask again. The raw token in the queue job conflicts with the brief's 'store only the hash' rule, so it is listed as an open question.

The brief says the worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, so one first try plus up to 3 retries. The backoff delays are not given, so they are unknown. After the last failure the worker logs the error and drops the job. Nobody is told, so the user gets no email and must ask again.

Opening the link only checks it. It does not use it. The link is used up only by a successful save, in the same transaction that stores the new hash and deletes the sessions. An invalid, expired or used token shows the same page: 'this link has expired, request a new one'. The page does not say which reason applies.

The server computes the SHA-256 hash of the token from the URL and looks up reset_tokens by token_hash, which should have a unique index. The row holds user_id, so the server knows the user. The token itself contains no user id.

Revoking sessions deletes every sessions row for the user. This includes the browser doing the reset, if it has a session. The user is not logged in after a reset. The redirect goes to the login page, as the brief says.

Yes, the token stays usable after a rejected password. The brief says the link works until it expires, and the token check runs before the password check, so a rejected password uses nothing. The source of the breached-password list is not stated in the brief or the existing system, so it is unknown. It is listed as an open question.

questions.text: Step 1 starts with an email and finds the user by email, and the hash only exists after the token is made. Which step finds the user from the hash, and is this note about step 1 or steps 2 and 3?
questions.about: Notes: 'The token holds no user id. Step 1 finds the user from the hash.'

questions.text: The diagram says 'fewer than 3 rows' passes, but an earlier answer said 'over 3 means stop'. Is the fourth request in an hour refused, or the third?
questions.about: 1 REQUEST LINK: fewer than 3 rows in last hour?

questions.text: How does the token get from the opened link to the form submit in step 3? Does the form carry it, or does the user have to open the link again?
questions.about: 3 SET PASSWORD: token -> hash -> row valid?

questions.text: If a user has other unused links still valid when a reset succeeds, do those links still work afterwards?
questions.about: 3 SET PASSWORD: in one transaction, store new hash, mark row used, delete the user's sessions

questions.text: What does the worker do with the raw token in a job once the email is sent or the job is dropped? Is the job removed from the queue at that point?
questions.about: Send email: Worker retries up to 3 times with backoff

questions.text: If the save succeeds but the 'password changed' email cannot be queued, what does the user see? Does the redirect to login still happen?
questions.about: 3 SET PASSWORD: Save fails: nothing changes, link stays usable

answers.text: The note was wrong about step 1. Step 1 finds the user by email. Steps 2 and 3 find the row, and so the user, from the token's hash. The note now says that, and the step text matches it.

The fourth request in an hour is refused. The count runs before the new row is inserted, so 0, 1 or 2 existing rows allow a request and 3 or more refuse it. This matches the brief's at-most-3 rule. My earlier 'over 3 means stop' was wrong, and the file now says '3 or more means stop'.

The form posts back to the same link address, so the token travels in the URL and the user never reopens the link. I did not use a hidden field, because the brief says the token appears only inside the link. The second check on submit still reads the token from the URL.

No other unused link can exist. Issuing a link revokes every older unused row, so at most one link is unused at any time. When a reset succeeds, the row being used is the only unused one. No new rule is added. The file now says that at most one link is unused at a time.

The brief implies a sent job is removed, and a dropped job is removed after the last failed try. It does not say how the queue or the worker logs keep or delete the job data after that. It is not known whether a copy of the raw token stays in queue storage or logs. This is listed under open questions, together with the question of keeping the link out of logs.

The reset stands and the user is still redirected to login. The save commits before the email is queued, so a failed queue does not undo the reset. The user sees no sign of the failed email, and the error is logged. This matches step 1's handling of a queue failure. The brief does not require a retry, so none is added.

teachbacks.text:
1. REQUEST LINK (user submits email on "Forgot password"). The API server receives the email address and looks the user up by email in Postgres (users table). If no user exists, it returns the generic message and stops. The generic message is identical for unknown email, over-limit and sent-link cases, so the caller cannot tell them apart.
2. Still in step 1, the API counts the user's reset_tokens rows created in the last hour, counting used and revoked rows too. The count runs before the new row exists. If it is 3 or more, it returns the generic message and stops. So requests 1 to 3 in an hour send a link and the 4th is refused.
3. The API makes 32 random bytes (the token), encodes them for use in a URL, and computes the SHA-256 hash of the raw bytes. Only the hash is stored.
4. In one transaction in Postgres, the API revokes the user's older unused reset_tokens rows (sets revoked_at) and inserts a new row: hash, created_at, expires_at = created_at + 30 minutes, empty used_at and revoked_at. The row links to the user. Because of the revoke, at most one link is unused at a time and an older link can never work again.
5. The API puts a reset email job into the email queue. The job holds the link containing the raw token. The API replies with the generic message after queueing, not after the email is actually sent. If the queue is down, it still returns the generic message and logs the error. The new row just expires unused and the user must ask again.
6. SEND EMAIL (existing worker, step 4 in the document). The worker starts when a job is in the queue. It sends the job via the mail provider and removes a sent job from the queue. The queue holds the raw token until the job is sent or dropped. If sending fails, it retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. Nobody is told, so the user gets no email and must request again.
7. OPEN LINK (user clicks the link in the email). The token comes from the URL. The server hashes it and looks up the reset_tokens row by hash. The row identifies the user, since the token holds no user id. If the row exists and is not expired, not used and not revoked, the server shows the "choose a new password" form. Otherwise it shows the expired page ("this link has expired, request a new one"), which is the same page for every failure reason. This step is read only. Opening a link never uses it.
8. SET PASSWORD (user submits the form). The form posts back to the same link address, so the token is still in the URL. The server re-hashes it and runs the same validity check. If that fails, it shows the expired page.
9. The server checks the new password: at least 12 characters and not on the breached-password list. If it fails, the form is shown again and the link stays usable.
10. If the password passes, in one transaction the server stores the new password hash in users, marks the reset_tokens row used, and deletes all of the user's sessions rows, which logs out every device. If the save fails, nothing changes and the link stays usable.
11. The server queues a "password changed" confirmation email, which the worker sends as in step 6, and redirects to the login page. The user is not logged in automatically. If queueing fails, the reset still stands because the transaction already committed. The user is still redirected, the error is logged and no confirmation is sent.
gaps: How the user is told or shown the result of a failed password check on the form (what message appears) is not stated, only that the form is shown again.
How 'valid' is checked precisely when expired, used and revoked all appear on the row (for example how the current time is compared to expires_at) is not given beyond the three conditions.
How the breached-password list is checked (source, refresh) is an open question, so how step 9 decides 'breached' is unexplained.
What the worker's backoff delays are is not stated, so the timing of retries in step 6 is unknown.
Whether the queue or worker logs keep a copy of the job (and so the raw token) is unknown.
